source: CARDI (Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute), "ការគ្រប់គ្រងជីជាតិដីលើដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Soil Fertility Management for Rice in Cambodia), 2nd printing, 2010 - no elibrary URL visible on the scanned copy
text:
Compost (ជីកំប៉ុស្ត៍) is made by layering and rotting down plant residues, animal manure, and household organic waste until it turns into a dark, crumbly, nutrient-rich soil amendment. Making and using compost improves soil structure and fertility, helps the soil hold water and nutrients better, cuts down how much chemical fertilizer a farmer needs to buy, and helps offset soil toxicity problems.

Materials needed: compost needs a mix of two kinds of ingredients. 'Dry'/carbon-rich material (ធាតុសើម) such as rice straw, dried grass, chaff, and dried leaves; and 'wet'/nitrogen-rich material such as fresh green leaves (especially from legumes/beans, ពពួកសំបូរអាសូត), fresh animal manure (លាមកសត្វ), and kitchen scraps. A thin layer of soil or already-finished compost is added between layers as well, both to add weight and to 'seed' the pile with the organisms that break the material down.

Keys to success: a good balance of dry and wet material (too much dry material slows rotting; too much wet material makes the pile soggy, which can turn it anaerobic and foul-smelling and lose nitrogen as ammonia), keeping air moving through the pile, keeping the pile evenly moist (not soaked, not dried out), and keeping it warm — a well-built pile noticeably heats up within about 1-2 days as decomposition gets going.

Method: choose a shaded site near a water source with good drainage, not a low spot where water collects. Build the pile in layers: a layer of dry/carbon-rich material (roughly 3 parts), then a layer of wet/nitrogen-rich material (roughly 2 parts), then a thin layer of soil or finished compost (roughly 0.5-1 part) on top; repeat the layering until the pile is about 1.5-2 meters wide and about 1 meter tall. Some farmers sprinkle in a small amount of urea or DAP fertilizer to speed up decomposition, which is optional but can help. Cover the top of the pile (with thatch or similar) to protect it from heavy rain and help it retain heat, while leaving the sides open enough for airflow. Water the pile lightly and regularly to keep it moist. Turn the pile after about 3 weeks — moving outer and bottom material into the center and vice versa — to keep decomposition even, then continue watering. Compost is generally ready to use after about 4-5 weeks total, once it has turned dark brown, has a crumbly soil-like texture, and no longer smells strongly.

Using compost: it can be broadcast lightly onto the seedbed and worked into the top few centimeters of soil, or worked into the field before transplanting. It can also be steeped in water, with the resulting liquid used to water and strengthen seedlings before transplanting.

Things to avoid: material that will not break down easily, such as woody stems or ornamental shrub trimmings; letting the pile go completely airless, which causes bad odor and nutrient loss; and letting the pile get too wet or too dry without correcting it.
